How accounts receivable arises: selling on credit (the practice), with an original example (Northline Print & Design)
The asset view: receivables are assets — future cash expected; assets referenced as a sibling topic only
Collecting: invoices, payment terms, and follow-up — each named generally
The risk: some customers never pay — the honest note; bad debts named
Aging receivables: sorting what customers owe by how long it has been owed, described in words
The honest framing: a sale on credit is a promise to pay — the business watches both the sale and the promise

claims.claim: Accounts receivable is money customers owe the business for goods or services already delivered — in OpenStax's terms, an outstanding customer debt on a credit sale.
Accounts receivable arises from selling on credit: the business provides the goods or service now and bills the customer for payment later, under credit payment terms.

A credit sale is recorded as revenue when the performance obligation is satisfied — whether or not payment has been received — and the unpaid amount is recorded as accounts receivable; no additional revenue is recorded when the receivable is later collected.

Accounts receivable is considered an asset: the business expects to receive payment within its operating period (less than a year), and the receivable sits on the asset side of the balance sheet, whose structure is the accounting equation assets = liabilities + equity.

The collection process rests on invoices (the bill naming what was delivered and when payment is due), payment terms (how long the customer has to pay, such as net 30), and follow-up (reminders and stronger measures when a customer is late).

Some customers never pay: receivables that the business does not expect to collect are called bad debts, and businesses account for uncollectible accounts through the direct write-off method or the allowance method, which estimates uncollectible amounts in advance via an allowance for doubtful accounts.

Aging receivables means sorting what customers owe by how long each invoice has been owed — into past-due categories such as current, 31 to 60, 61 to 90, and over 90 days — to guide follow-up, flag credit risk, and estimate uncollectible amounts.

The honest framing: a sale on credit is a promise to pay. The business watches both the sale (revenue earned at delivery) and the promise (the receivable, which stays on the books until cash arrives).

Accounts receivable and accounts payable are mirror images of the same kind of transaction: money owed to the business is a receivable (asset), while money the business owes its suppliers after purchasing on credit is an accounts payable (liability).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is a receivable really an asset if some customers never pay?
positions: A receivable is counted at its full face value because the business delivered the goods or services and is entitled to the money.
A portion of receivables is expected to go uncollected, so counting the full amount overstates the cash the business will actually receive.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both positions are true in sequence. The business records the full receivable and estimates the uncollectible portion separately: under the allowance method (OpenStax Section 9.2), an allowance for doubtful accounts reduces receivables to net realizable value — the amount anticipated to be collected — while the business still tries to collect the entire amount owed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: When should uncollectible amounts be recognized — when they happen or in advance?
positions: Direct write-off: remove a specific account from receivables only when it clearly fails to pay.
Allowance method: estimate expected losses in advance and match them to the period's sales.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: OpenStax Section 9.2: the allowance method is the more widely used approach because it satisfies the matching principle, while the direct write-off method is used mainly by small sellers for which credit is not a significant part of sales.
